title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: After the encounter at Vyazma—where Kutuzov had been unable to hold back his troops in their eagerness to overwhelm and cut off the enemy, and so on—the farther movement of the fleeing French and the Russians pursuing them continued as far as Krasnoe without a battle. The flight was so rapid that the Russian army pursuing the French could not keep up; cavalry and artillery horses broke down, and the information about French movements was never reliable.
The men in the Russian army were so worn out by this continuous marching at twenty-seven miles a day that they simply could not go any faster.

To understand the degree of exhaustion of the Russian army, you only need to grasp clearly the meaning of one fact: while losing no more than five thousand killed and wounded after Tarutino, and fewer than a hundred prisoners, the Russian army that had left Tarutino a hundred thousand strong reached Krasnoe with only fifty thousand.

The rapid Russian pursuit was just as destructive to our army as the French flight was to theirs. The only difference was that the Russian army moved voluntarily, with no such threat of destruction as hung over the French, and that sick Frenchmen were left behind in enemy hands while sick Russians were left among their own people. The main cause of Napoleon's army wasting away was the speed of its movement, and convincing proof of this is the corresponding decline of the Russian army.

As far as it was in his power, Kutuzov did not try to check the French movement, though that was what Petersburg and the Russian generals wanted. Instead, as he had at Tarutino and Vyazma, he directed all his efforts toward speeding the retreat along while easing the movement of our army.

But besides this, since the army's exhaustion and enormous reduction from the speed of the advance had become obvious, another reason for slackening the pace and delaying presented itself: the aim of the Russian army was to pursue the French. The French route was unknown, so the closer our troops trod on their heels, the greater the distance they had to cover. Only by keeping some distance back could they cut across the French zigzag path. All the artful maneuvers suggested by our generals meant fresh movements of the army and a lengthening of its marches, whereas the only sensible objective was to shorten those marches. To this end, Kutuzov directed his efforts throughout the entire campaign from Moscow to Vilna—not casually or intermittently, but so consistently that he never once deviated from it.

Kutuzov felt and knew—not through reasoning or military science, but with the whole of his Russian being—what every Russian soldier felt: that the French were beaten, that the enemy was fleeing and must be driven out; but at the same time he, like his soldiers, understood all the hardship of this march, the rapidity of which was unparalleled for such a time of the year.

But the generals—especially the foreign ones in the Russian army—wanted to distinguish themselves, astonish someone, and for some reason capture a king or a duke. Any battle now would be horrible and senseless, yet to them this seemed the perfect time to fight and conquer somebody. Kutuzov merely shrugged his shoulders when one after another they presented him with maneuver plans for soldiers who were ill-shod, insufficiently clad, and half-starved—soldiers who within a month, without fighting a single battle, had dwindled to half their original number and who, at the best, if the flight continued, would have to go a greater distance than they had already traversed before they reached the frontier.
This desire to distinguish themselves, to maneuver, to overthrow and cut off showed itself most clearly whenever the Russians stumbled on the French army.

So it was at Krasnoe, where they expected to find one of the three French columns but instead ran into Napoleon himself with sixteen thousand men. Despite all of Kutuzov's efforts to avoid this ruinous encounter and preserve his troops, the slaughter of the broken French mob by exhausted Russians continued at Krasnoe for three days.

Toll wrote out a battle plan: "The first column will march to such and such a place," and so on. And as usual, nothing happened according to plan. Prince Eugene of Wurttemberg fired from a hilltop over the French crowds running past and demanded reinforcements that never arrived. The French, avoiding the Russians, scattered and hid in the forest by night, making their way around as best they could, and continued their flight.

Miloradovich, who said he did not want to know anything about the commissary affairs of his detachment and could never be found when needed—this man who styled himself chevalier sans peur et sans reproche, "the knight without fear and without reproach," and who loved to parley with the French—sent envoys demanding their surrender, wasted time, and didn't do what he was ordered to do.
* Knight without fear and without reproach.
"I give you that column, lads," he said, riding up to his troops and pointing out the French to the cavalry.

And the cavalry, with spurs and sabers urging on horses that could barely move, trotted with great effort to the column presented to them—that is, to a crowd of Frenchmen frozen stiff, frostbitten, and starving—and the column that had been presented to them threw down its arms and surrendered, as it had long been anxious to do.

At Krasnoe they took twenty-six thousand prisoners, several hundred cannon, and a stick called a "marshal's staff," and they argued about who had distinguished himself and congratulated themselves on their achievement—while deeply regretting that they hadn't captured Napoleon, or at least a marshal or some kind of hero, and blaming one another and especially Kutuzov for having failed to do so.

These men, carried away by their passions, were nothing more than blind tools of the most melancholy law of necessity, yet they considered themselves heroes and imagined they were accomplishing a most noble and honorable deed. They blamed Kutuzov, saying that from the very start of the campaign he had prevented them from defeating Napoleon, that he thought of nothing but satisfying his passions and would not advance from the Linen Factories because he was comfortable there, that he had stopped the advance at Krasnoe because he quite lost his head on learning Napoleon was there, and that he probably had an understanding with Napoleon and had been bribed, and so on and so on.

Not only his contemporaries, carried away by their passions, but posterity and history itself have acclaimed Napoleon as grand, while Kutuzov is described by foreigners as a crafty, dissolute, weak old courtier, and by Russians as something indefinite—a sort of puppet useful only because he had a Russian name.
